```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
```

# Airbnb
```{r}
data("nyc_airbnb")

nyc_airbnb = 
  nyc_airbnb |> 
  mutate( 
    starts = review_scores_location / 2
  ) |> 
  rename(
    borough = neighborhood
  ) |> 
  filter(
    borough != "Staten Island"
  ) |> 
  select(
    price, stars, borough, room_type
  )

nyc_airbnb
```

#linear regression
```{r}
fit = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb)
```

What we have
```{r}
fit
summary(fit)
coef(fit)

fitted.values(fit)
resid(fit)
names(summary(fit))
```

Names of things in fit
  -some stuff that goes along: what is rank, what is df residual, etc
Linear model saves a bunch of stuff in the background - helpful to know its their

most of the output is bad, but sometimes it's useful

```{r}
broom::tidy(fit) |> 
  select(-std.error) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

broom::glance(fit)
```
-broom function super useful, broom pulls out this useful information
  -broom useful for anything
  
  -broom::glance(fit) - gives you very quick look at information that is helpful. 
  
Change reference category
```{r}
fit=
  nyc_airbnb |> 
  mutate(
    borough = fct_infreq(borough)
  ) |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = _)

broom::tidy(fit) |> 
  select(-std.error) |> 
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough:"))
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
  
  
  ##Diagnostics
  
  diagnostics is basically "look at the residuals"
  
```{r}
modelr::add_residuals(nyc_airbnb, fit)
```
Adding in a column called resid: worry about residuals and residual distribution
  We can look at residuals
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  modelr::add_residuals(fit) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = stars, y = resid)) +
  geom_point()

nyc_airbnb |> 
  modelr::add_residuals(fit) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = borough, y = resid)) +
  geom_violoin()
```
Residuals are skewed:
  -much more spread in 5 stars vs 3 stars

With regression with large samples everything becomes equally distributed
  -shouldn't trust CI that come out of this

## Hypothesis testing

```{r}
broom::tidy(fit) |> 
  mutate(term = str_replace(term, "borough", "Borough: ")) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Permutation testing - when you don't trust the assumptions you should use this
Is brough significant: can't look at individual values need to look at whole thing

Try testing nested model

```{r}
fit_null = lm(price ~ stars, data = nyc_airbnb)
fit_alt = lm(price ~ stars + borough, data = nyc_airbnb)
  
  anova(vit_null, fit_alt)
```


## Nesting data
different from nesting models - 
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  lm(price ~ stars * borough + room_type, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy() |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
looking at relation
does stars differ if its in brooklyn vs manhattan
  -how does reference of room tiype differ from reference category:
    -shared room type for Manhattan
    
What if I want to know what's happening in Manhattan?

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Manhattan") |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy()

nyc_airbnb |> 
  filter(borough == "Bronx") |> 
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = _) |> 
  broom::tidy()
```

If we want to do this over and over again have to do the 5 boroughs

Fix this with iteration
```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough)

airbnb_lm = function(data) {
  
  lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = data)
}
```


```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |> 
  mutate(fits = map(datasets, airbnb_lm))
```
by bourgh fits linear models to data

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |> 
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, airbnb_lm),
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |> 
  pull(results)

nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |> 
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, airbnb_lm),
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |> 
  select(-datasets, -fits) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  select(borough, term, estimate) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  )

```

Before create one fucntion and plugs in input where it's supposed to go, happens often enough that 
  -create anonymous function 
  -puts argument and 

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |> 
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, \data() lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data = data)),
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |> 
  pull(results)

nyc_airbnb |> 
  nest(datasets = -borough) |> 
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, airbnb_lm),
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |> 
  select(-datasets, -fits) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  select(borough, term, estimate) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  )

```

```{r}
nyc_airbnb |> 
  filteR(borough == "linear_models.Rmdanhattan") |> 
  nest(datasets = -neighborhood) |> 
  mutate(
    fits = map(datasets, \(df) lm(price ~ stars + room_type, data =df)),
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |> 
  select(neighborhood, results) |> 
  unnest(resutls) |> 
  filter(term == "room_typePrivate room") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = neighborhood, y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 80, hjust = 1))
```
nest data according to neighborhood, tidy up with broom tidy, look at results: is room vs entire apartment different in Manhattan

working the way I'm excpecting to: data sets fits column and results column
  -one factor could be dropping between different neighborhoods
  
## Logistic regression

```{r}
baltimore_df = 
  read_csv("data/homicide-data.csv") |> 
  filter(city == "Baltimore") |> 
  mutate(
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)
  )
baltimore_df
```


Fit the logistic regression

```{r}
fit_logistic = 
  baltimore_df |> 
  mutate(victim_race = fct_infreq(victim_race)) |> 
  glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_race, data = _, family = binomial())



fit_logistic |> 
  broom::tidy() |> 
  mutate(OR = exp(estimate)) |> 
  select(term, OR, estimate, p.value) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Binomial just goes with logistic regression
